title: Chemistry of Household & Personal Care Products

competencies.text: Construct a table using product labels (bleach, detergents, baking powder, shampoo, soap, toothpaste).
Explain benefits and risks of household products by referring to DTI, FDA, and DENR guidelines.

days.title: Reading Product Labels
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will construct a table from product labels (bleach, detergent, baking powder, shampoo, soap, toothpaste) and explain their benefits and risks using DTI, FDA and DENR guidelines.

🏷️ What a Good Label Shows

  • Product name and brand, and the net content (mL or g).
  • Active ingredients — the chemicals that do the job — and often their concentration.
  • Directions for use and warnings / precautions (e.g., "Keep out of reach of children," "Do not mix with other cleaners").
  • First-aid instructions in case of swallowing or contact with eyes.
  • Manufacturer or distributor, batch or lot number, expiry date.
  • FDA registration/notification number for cosmetics, drugs and household hazardous products.

📋 Building a Product Table

For each product, record: product, active ingredient, what it does, how to use safely, risk if misused, how to dispose. Organizing labels this way makes it easy to compare products and spot dangers — for example, two cleaners that must never be mixed.

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: On a bleach label, which part tells you the chemical that actually disinfects?

choices.label: The active ingredient list
The brand name and its logo
The net content in mL
The barcode on the back

scenario.explanation: The active ingredient (sodium hypochlorite for bleach) is the chemical that does the job. Brand, volume and barcode do not tell you that.

scenario.text: A label says "Do not mix with ammonia or acids." Why is this warning important?

choices.label: Mixing can release toxic gases
Mixing makes the product too weak
Mixing changes the product color
Mixing makes the bottle too heavy

scenario.explanation: Bleach reacts with ammonia (chloramine gas) and with acids (chlorine gas). Both gases damage the lungs.

scenario.text: You are making a table of household products. Which set of columns is MOST useful for safety?

choices.label: Active ingredient, use, risk, disposal
Brand, price, color, bottle shape
Store, cashier, date, payment type
Scent, size, logo and advertising slogan

scenario.explanation: Knowing what is inside, what it does, what can go wrong and how to dispose of it lets you use and store each product safely.

days.title: The Chemistry Inside
days.content:
🧪 Six Common Products

ProductActive ingredientHow it works
BleachSodium hypochlorite (NaClO)Strong oxidizer; destroys germs and stains
DetergentSurfactants (e.g., sodium lauryl sulfate), buildersSurfactants surround grease so water can rinse it away
Baking powderSodium bicarbonate + an acidReact when wet and heated, releasing CO₂ bubbles
ShampooMild surfactants, conditionersRemoves oil from hair gently
SoapSodium/potassium salts of fatty acidsOne end grabs oil, the other water
ToothpasteFluoride, mild abrasivesFluoride strengthens enamel; abrasives scrub plaque

🧼 How Soap and Detergent Clean

Soap and surfactant molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail. The tails dig into grease; the heads face the water. The grease is trapped in tiny balls (micelles) that rinse away. Water alone cannot do this because oil and water do not mix.

🍰 Baking Powder

Baking soda (a base) + an acid + water → carbon dioxide gas. The bubbles make cakes and puto rise.

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each product or term to its chemistry. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.why: It destroys germs and colored stains by oxidizing them.
Surfactants let water carry oily dirt away.

match.right: Releases CO₂ to make dough rise
match.why: Bicarbonate and acid react when wet and heated.
Fluoride makes tooth enamel more resistant to acid.
This structure lets soap connect oil to water.

match.right: Tiny ball of soap trapping grease
match.why: Grease inside micelles rinses away with water.

match.right: Mild surfactants for hair and scalp
match.why: Gentler surfactants clean without stripping hair too much.
Fine particles in toothpaste clean the tooth surface.

days.title: Benefits and Risks
days.content:
⚖️ Every Product Has Both

ProductBenefitRisk if misused
BleachDisinfects, whitensToxic gas if mixed with ammonia or acid; burns skin and eyes
DetergentRemoves greaseSkin irritation; phosphates feed algae in rivers
ToothpastePrevents cavitiesToo much swallowed fluoride can spot children's teeth
Shampoo / soapHygieneEye irritation, allergies to fragrances or preservatives

☠️ Never Mix

  • Bleach + ammonia (some glass cleaners) → chloramine gas
  • Bleach + acids (vinegar, toilet bowl cleaners) → chlorine gas

🌊 Environmental Risk: Eutrophication

Phosphates and nitrates from detergents and fertilizers act as nutrients for algae. Algae grow into a thick green layer, block sunlight, then die. Bacteria decomposing them use up the dissolved oxygen, and fish die. This is eutrophication. Choosing phosphate-free detergents and not dumping wash water into canals helps.

🛟 First Aid Basics

If a chemical gets in the eyes: rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes. If swallowed: do not induce vomiting; bring the label and go to the nearest health center.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Weigh benefits and risks in real situations. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: While cleaning the bathroom, your cousin wants to mix bleach with a toilet bowl cleaner (an acid) "to make it stronger." What should you do?

choices.label: Stop her — the mixture releases chlorine gas
Let her — it doubles the cleaning power
Stop her — the bleach will lose its strong smell
Let her — acids make bleach safer to use

scenario.explanation: Bleach reacts with acids to give off toxic chlorine gas, which can seriously hurt the lungs, especially in a small bathroom.

scenario.text: A creek near a laundry area is covered with thick green algae and fish are dying. Which cause is MOST likely?

choices.label: Phosphates from detergent water feeding algae
Soap bubbles blocking sunlight for fish
Cold rinse water lowering the creek's temperature
Shampoo fragrance poisoning the algae

scenario.explanation: Phosphates are nutrients for algae. When the algae die, decomposers use up the oxygen in the water, and fish suffocate (eutrophication).

scenario.text: A mother gives her 3-year-old a long strip of toothpaste and lets him swallow it daily. What is the main concern?

choices.label: Too much fluoride can spot developing teeth
Toothpaste has no benefit for young children
The abrasives will dissolve his tooth enamel
Fluoride makes children's teeth grow faster

scenario.explanation: Fluoride protects teeth, but swallowing too much while teeth are forming can cause white spots (dental fluorosis). A pea-sized amount is advised.

scenario.text: A cake came out flat. The baker used old baking powder that had been stored in a damp place. Which explanation fits BEST?

choices.label: It had already reacted and lost its CO₂
It had turned into salt and sugar
Moisture made it release far too much CO₂ later
Damp storage made it more acidic

scenario.explanation: Baking powder releases CO₂ when it gets wet. If it absorbed moisture in storage, it reacted early, leaving little gas to raise the cake.

scenario.text: Bleach splashes into your classmate's eye. What is the BEST first action?

choices.label: Rinse the eye with clean running water for 15 minutes
Rub the eye gently with a towel to remove the bleach
Put vinegar in the eye to neutralize the bleach
Cover the eye and wait until the stinging stops

scenario.explanation: Flushing with plenty of clean water removes and dilutes the chemical. Rubbing spreads it; adding another chemical can make the injury worse.

days.title: Rules That Protect Us: DTI, FDA, DENR
days.content:
🏛️ Three Agencies, Three Jobs

AgencyWhat it does for household products
FDA PhilippinesRegisters or notifies cosmetics, drugs and household/urban hazardous substances; checks safety and labeling; issues advisories on unregistered or unsafe products
DTIEnforces product standards (PS/ICC marks) and fair labeling; protects consumers from misleading claims
DENR (through EMB)Regulates the handling and disposal of hazardous chemicals and waste; sets limits on what may be discharged into water

🛒 Smart Buying

Choose products with a valid FDA registration/notification and complete labels in English or Filipino. Avoid repacked chemicals in unlabeled bottles — you cannot know what is inside or how to treat an accident.

♻️ Safe Storage and Disposal

  • Keep products in their original labeled containers, closed, away from food and children.
  • Never store chemicals in soft-drink bottles.
  • Do not pour leftover strong chemicals into canals or rivers; follow the label and barangay collection for household hazardous waste.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

escape.text: What is the active ingredient in household bleach?

choices.label: Sodium hypochlorite
Sodium hydrogen carbonate
Sodium chloride
Sodium fluoride

escape.explanation: Bleach is a solution of sodium hypochlorite (NaClO), a strong oxidizer. Bicarbonate is baking soda, chloride is table salt, fluoride is in toothpaste.

escape.text: Which Philippine agency registers cosmetics such as shampoo before they are sold?

choices.label: Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
Department of Trade and Industry (DTI)
Department of Environment (DENR)
Department of Education (DepEd)

escape.explanation: The FDA evaluates and registers or notifies cosmetics, drugs and household hazardous products for safety and correct labeling.

escape.text: Which agency regulates how hazardous chemical waste is disposed of to protect rivers?

choices.label: DENR — Environment
DTI — Trade and Industry
FDA — Food and Drugs
DOH — Health and hospitals

escape.explanation: DENR, through its Environmental Management Bureau, sets rules on hazardous waste and limits on what may be discharged into water.

escape.text: Why can soap remove oily dirt that water alone cannot?

choices.label: Its molecules link oil to water
It makes the water much hotter
It turns oil into solid crystals
It makes the oil evaporate faster

escape.explanation: Soap molecules have an oil-loving tail and a water-loving head, so they trap grease in micelles that water can rinse away.

choices.label: Too many nutrients cause algae growth and oxygen loss
Water becoming much cleaner after soap is added to it
Fish multiplying because of extra nitrogen gas
Rivers drying up because detergents absorb water

escape.explanation: Excess phosphates and nitrates feed algae; when they die, decomposers use up oxygen, harming fish and other life.

escape.text: A neighbor sells cleaning liquid repacked in unlabeled soft-drink bottles. What is the BIGGEST danger?

choices.label: Someone may drink it or mix it unsafely
It will cost more than the branded product
It will clean more slowly than usual
It will make the bottle melt quickly

escape.explanation: Without a label you cannot know the ingredients, warnings or first aid, and a soft-drink bottle invites accidental drinking, especially by children.
